headline: The editor was telling agents the wrong size limits for a level's background — one too generous, one too tight.
matters: A background picture has a hard ceiling on how many unique tiles it can use, set by where the console keeps its sprite table. The editor told agents that ceiling was higher than it really is, so an agent could build a background the console physically cannot hold and only find out later, at bake time or as garbage sprayed over the sprites. In the same breath it was too strict about height: it insisted every background be half the height the engine actually supports, which made a full-height background impossible to author through the agent path at all — even though backgrounds that size already exist in the library. Both numbers now come from the shared file that records what the engine really does, so the limit the editor enforces, the limit it advertises and the limit the engine holds are one number that cannot drift apart. Before this there was not a single test anywhere covering reading or writing a background through the agent path; there are now, and I checked them by breaking the code on purpose and confirming the right ones failed. The one thing left unproven is a full-height background making the whole trip through a real save and into the engine's own tooling — that needs the app running, so I have written it down rather than implying the tests covered it.

headline: I tried to build a ROM with a moving background band. It doesn't build — and finding out why was the point.
matters: Nobody had ever put an editor-made animated background into an actual ROM, so nobody knew what would happen. I did, and it stops in two places, both on the engine side. First, the engine's tool writes a reference to the animation artwork in a form the assembler won't accept — I found the correct form by looking at a neighbouring file doing the same job, and confirmed it fixes that step. Second, the table that decides how much room each piece of the ROM gets allots this feature exactly two bytes, because two bytes is what the switched-off version takes up; a real band needs about eight thousand. Neither problem is ours and neither could have been found any other way than by trying. Along the way I told you two things that were wrong: that there was spare room nearby (there isn't — what looked like spare room is other artwork, including the very background tiles this whole effort has been about), and that the knock-on effect was contained (it isn't, though it turned out smaller than feared — five pieces shift, not fifteen, because a sound-related address is pinned in hardware and absorbs the rest). The engine lane is doing both fixes as one job. When it lands I run this again and you finally get to watch the background move.

headline: A finding I sent another lane last night was wrong about its own cause, and chasing that down found the real one: our test builds are not as repeatable as everyone assumed.
matters: When we pin a copy of the game's code to measure against, we do not pin the tool that builds it — so the same unchanged code can build into a different ROM hours later, with nothing on screen to say why. headline: Swept about 1,200 dead X-server leftovers off the machine; the harnesses that leak them are still unfixed.
matters: Test runs had been leaking a virtual display each and never cleaning up, so the machine was carrying 20 dead servers and roughly 1,200 orphaned lock and socket files, and each new run had to climb past them to find a free number. Nothing was lost and your own desktop session was never touched. This removed the mess, not the cause: four launcher scripts still leak on every run, so it will come back.
detail: O20 first half, foreground (agents cannot do process work). All 20 Xvfb had been reparented to systemd --user, were 8.5-35 h old, and every one had zero client fds; killed by PID individually, never pkill. Residue was far larger than the booked row: 943 locks / 264 sockets against ONE live X server (Xwayland :0), hence display numbers climbing to :1030. Removed 941 locks + 263 sockets with a live-PID guard, keeping :0. The guard held back :151, whose recorded PID had been RECYCLED onto a Vivaldi renderer thread - so a PID-liveness check on a lock file is two-valued ('that PID is in use' != 'that X server runs'), the same family as [ -S socket ] reporting a corpse as a server. Removed it on the stronger instrument: wrong process class plus no socket. Cause (4 unguarded launchers) open.

headline: Fix a chunk once and every copy of it in the level fixes itself — with a checkbox for the copies you want left alone.
matters: This finishes what you asked for. Stamping remembers by default, so correcting a chunk corrects the whole level; ticking the box makes a stamp a plain copy that nothing will touch again, and you can detach one you already placed. Hand-painting over part of a stamp detaches only the tiles you painted, so your touch-ups are never overwritten. Proven by driving the real editor and clicking the real controls, not by unit tests — the tests cannot see the screen. One limit worth knowing: copies stamped in OTHER acts keep their link but are not updated yet.

headline: Our test harnesses have been quietly burning display numbers for five days, and the guard we added last week is what made it certain.
matters: 1,500 stale directories and 100 dead lock files had built up since the 25th, and every leaked lock permanently burns an X display number so every later test run scans longer before it can start. It is now cleaned up automatically as each run ends. The residue already on the machine is still there and still growing — from other projects' test runs, not this one.
detail: O20+O23, merge 055bff40 pushed. Cause: /usr/bin/xvfb-run has no trap, so its whole cleanup sits after the command line and is skipped whenever the wrapper is signalled — which is what killTree does on every teardown, so O16's orphan fix guaranteed this leak. Two leak rates, the uncounted one 17x the counted: tempdirs leak on every teardown, locks/sockets only on abrupt ones. Both rows were wrong: no .sh starts an X server (the four unguarded launchers are .mjs), and two .sh DO launch by proxy. reapDisplays() is scoped to artifacts named by processes inside a tree the harness launched. THE PARCEL'S REAL LESSON: boundSocketPaths() failed OPEN against its own docstring — an empty Set meant both 'I could not look' and 'nothing is bound', so gate 3 would invert from a refusal into a permission and leave the never-reap list as the only thing protecting the owner's desktop socket; latent, not live. Found by an overseer poison that came back GREEN because gate 3 was covering for gate 1. Now a null sentinel read as gate 0, refuse everything loudly. Two further poisons re-planted independently by the overseer post-fix, each firing in exactly one row. A third silently no-op'd against a changed declaration and returned a clean 20/20 — proof-the-edit-landed is now the rule before any plant is believed. A world px and a plane px are different units and the exchange rate is the parallax factor, per band horizontally and per scene vertically -- so comparing 2048 to 512 is a category error, not an arithmetic one. The row's 2,048 is the VERTICAL OVERSHOOT, traced to this repo's own BG capability survey row 11 (6144 act height - 4096 ceiling at v_factor 3), and it equals SECTION_PIXEL_SIZE BY ACCIDENT, which is why it reads as a wrap width once relayed without its axis.
